land.text: the RSFSR, whose territory the Russian Federation inherited: 'On 25 December 1991, following the dissolution of the Soviet Union' (Russia page)

predecessors.note: The RSFSR dossier ends in December 1991 and names russian-federation as successor.

land.text: the Soviet Union's seat, Moscow, and its continuing international role passed to the Russian Federation; no land beyond the RSFSR's

predecessors.note: The 1992 Cliopatria shape is the RSFSR area only; the other Soviet republics became independent states.

correction.text: the Russian Federation as it stood when the Soviet Union dissolved: the 1992 Cliopatria shape used one year early

Chechnya stays a contest zone (ledger) and goes out of the shape in 1997.

correction.text: Russia without Chechnya for 1997-1999: Khasavyurt (31 August 1996) ended the war with 'preservation of Chechnya's de facto independence' and federal forces left by the end of 1996; the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria (Maskhadov elected January 1997) held the republic until the Russian ground advance of October 1999

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria draws Chechnya inside Russia in 1996-1999 and outside it in 1992-1995 and 2000-2005 - the wrong way round (compare the Chechen Republic row, 17,433 km2, years 1992-1995 and 2000-2005). The shape area (16.93 M) minus Chechnya is the 1992 shape. Years for this corrected shape: 1997-1999.

correction.text: Russia with Chechnya: 'The battle ended when the Russian army seized the city on 2 February 2000'; main phase ended 30 April 2000; the infobox records 'Chechnya reincorporated into Russia'

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria shows the Chechen Republic as a separate polity in 2000-2005 and leaves Chechnya out of the Russian shape. By 2000 Russia held the republic (direct rule from May 2000; Kadyrov's pro-Moscow government); the separatists continued an insurgency, not a territorial state. The Chechen Republic row (eu-19) should be reviewed in the same sense. Area 16.91 M km2 against 17.10 M (ratio 0.99).

16.93 M km2, the shape with Chechnya, for 2006-2013; against the infobox 17.10 M km2 (ratio 0.99). The infobox figure (17,098,246 km2) is qualified '(within internationally recognised borders)' (Russia page, reread 2026-11-01), which reads as leaving Crimea out (the page does not say so in words), so the pre-2014 shape compares with it directly and falls a little below it (corrected: an earlier version said the figure includes Crimea).

correction.text: the 2006-2013 shape continued: Crimea and Sevastopol (21,857 km2 in the Cliopatria 2014 shape) are taken out of the Russian solid and drawn as Russian-occupied land of Ukraine (hatched) by the ledger's occupation_start of February 2014; plus Chukotka east of 180 degrees, which the Cliopatria outline leaves out

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria adds Crimea to Russia in 2014 (16.926 M to 16.948 M km2) while the Ukraine row keeps it until 2023: a double claim. 'Russia formally incorporated Crimea on 18 March 2014'; UNGA resolution 68/262 of 27 March 2014 affirmed 'the territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognised borders'. The project's scope draws Crimea as occupied land, so the shape stays at the 2013 outline. Applies 2014-2023; the 2022 annexations are ledger events. Chukotka Autonomous Okrug page, opened 2 Nov 2026: 'is the easternmost federal subject of Russia', 'the only part of Russia lying partially in the Western Hemisphere', and 'Chukotka declared its separation to become a subject of the Russian Federation in its own right' (1991).

the Donetsk People's Republic with its 2022 gains, about 60% of Donetsk Oblast, annexed on 30 September 2022 (ledger gain from the Donetsk People's Republic)
the Chukotka Autonomous Okrug, including the part east of the 180th meridian, which the Cliopatria outline (bbox ends at longitude 180.0) leaves out

correction.text: the 2006-2013 outline plus the Luhansk and Donetsk People's Republics, which Russia annexed on 30 September 2022 ('On 30 September, Putin signed accession treaties with the four pro-Russian leaders of the regions'); Crimea and the occupied south stay out of the solid and are hatched occupation by the ledger; the Ukrainian foothold in Kursk Oblast (August 2024) is a ledger contest; plus Chukotka east of 180 degrees, which the Cliopatria outline leaves out

keyframe_review.note: Revised after review. The 2024 Cliopatria shape is identical to 2014's although Ukraine's Kursk incursion began in August 2024 ('captured an area of up to 350 square kilometres', a Ukrainian claim) and Russia claims four Ukrainian oblasts (about 15% of Ukraine's area, 'more than 90,000 km2'). The earlier correction was the bare 2013 outline, which contradicted the two September 2022 gains (the Luhansk and Donetsk People's Republics, which nothing takes away); the correction now adds those lands to the solid, so the shape agrees with the ledger and with the two republics' dissolve events. Crimea (the Crimea occupation event, 2014-2) and the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia holdings (the 2022-2 occupation of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia) stay hatched occupation of Ukraine, because they passed straight from Ukraine to Russian control, whereas the Donbas lands first formed two de facto states with their own dossiers; the author does not accept the reviewer's alternative of drawing Crimea solid as well, since the project scope draws it as occupied land. A renderer that wants one treatment for all annexed land can retype the two September 2022 gains as occupation_start with counterpart ukraine and drop the two union members. Revised by fx-41 (window request R147): Chukotka is added to the corrected shape, because Cliopatria's Russian Federation outlines stop at longitude 180.0 and about 400 cells of the okrug east of it would be dropped at this snap (the p1990-p1999 and p2000-p2009 patches already do the same for the 1991, 1992, 1995, 1996, 2000 and 2006 keyframes). Chukotka Autonomous Okrug page, opened 2 Nov 2026: 'is the easternmost federal subject of Russia', 'the only part of Russia lying partially in the Western Hemisphere', and 'Chukotka declared its separation to become a subject of the Russian Federation in its own right' (1991).

region.text: the Russian Federation, the former RSFSR, on its Moscow core and the whole of its 1992 extent

ledger.note: 1991: the Russian Federation emerges from the Soviet Union. 'On 25 December 1991, following the dissolution of the Soviet Union'; infobox 'Declaration of State Sovereignty: 12 June 1990', 'Belovezha Accords ratifed: 12 December 1991'. The state takes the whole RSFSR territory.

region.text: Transnistria, the left bank of the Dniester, listed as Russian-occupied 'since 1992'

ledger.note: 1992: the Transnistria War leaves Russian military presence on the Dniester. The page lists 'Transnistria, since 1992' among Russian-occupied territories; 'These differences erupted into the Transnistria War in 1992'; but Russia 'officially recognizes Moldovan sovereignty over Transnistria'. The land is drawn by the transnistria dossier; this is the occupation layer (page gives no month).

region.text: Chechnya, the republic Dudayev's government held as independent

ledger.note: 11 December 1994: Russian troops enter Chechnya. 'On 11 December 1994, approximately 40,000 Russian troops crossed the border into Chechnya'; infobox 11 December 1994 - 31 August 1996.

region.text: 'most of the republic' of Chechnya, taken in the conventional campaign

ledger.note: May 1995: Russian forces hold most of Chechnya. 'By May 1995, the Russian forces conquered most of the republic in the conventional campaign'; Grozny's battle 'continued until the official end on 6 March 1995'. The Chechen-held mountains remain contested.

region.text: Chechnya, ended by the Khasavyurt Accord

ledger.note: 31 August 1996: the Khasavyurt Accord ends the First Chechen War after separatist 'Operation Jihad' (6 August 1996) 'effectively reversing Russian gains'; it 'deferred the decision on Chechnya's status until 2001'.

region.text: Chechnya, vacated by federal forces under the Accord

ledger.note: End of 1996: Russian forces leave Chechnya. The Accord set the withdrawal of 'all federal forces from Chechnya by 31 December 1996'; the page does not confirm the completion date but the war ended with 'complete withdrawal' and 'preservation of Chechnya's de facto independence'; Maskhadov was elected president in January 1997 and signed a peace treaty with Yeltsin on 12 May 1997.

region.text: Chechnya north of the Terek, then the whole republic

ledger.note: October 1999: the second invasion of Chechnya. After the 7 August 1999 Dagestan incursion, 'Putin announced that Russian troops would initiate a land war' on 1 October; Russian forces 'reached the Terek River on 5 October 1999' and crossed it on 12 October.

region.text: Grozny, the capital of Chechnya

ledger.note: 2 February 2000: Grozny falls. 'The battle ended when the Russian army seized the city on 2 February 2000.'

region.text: the rest of Chechnya, its 'last populated centres of the organized resistance'

ledger.note: April 2000: the main phase ends and Chechnya is back under Russian rule. After the 23 April 2000 Serzhen-Yurt ambush, Russian forces 'seized the last populated centres of the organized resistance'; infobox 'Main phase: 7 August 1999 - 30 April 2000' and 'Chechnya reincorporated into Russia'; 'Russia established direct rule over Chechnya in May 2000'.

region.text: Chechnya, end of the main phase of the war

ledger.note: 30 April 2000: end of the main phase of the Second Chechen War; guerrilla fighting continues until the counter-terrorism regime ends on 16 April 2009 but holds no territory.

region.text: Abkhazia and South Ossetia, listed as Russian-occupied 'since 2008'

ledger.note: August 2008: Russia recognises and garrisons Abkhazia and South Ossetia. Medvedev 'signed decrees on 26 August 2008 recognizing the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia'; the page lists both as Russian-occupied 'since 2008'. The land is drawn by the republic-of-abkhazia and republic-of-south-ossetia dossiers; this is the occupation layer. The Russo-Georgian War page, reopened for the revision, dates the invasion to 8 August and the recognition to 26 August ('On 26 August, Medvedev issued orders recognising the two states'). The georgia dossier (eu-19) records these two lands as lost to the republics (georgia /ledger/16-17), not as Russian-occupied, so this event has no georgia mirror; the buffer-zone occupation just below is the one georgia mirrors.

region.text: the Georgian towns Russian forces held outside Abkhazia and South Ossetia in August 2008: Gori, Zugdidi, Senaki and Poti

ledger.note: 8 August 2008: Russian forces invade Georgia's undisputed territory. The page says Russia 'launched a full-scale land, air and sea invasion of Georgia, including its undisputed territory, on 8 August' and that 'Zugdidi, Senaki, Poti, and Gori were temporarily occupied by Russia' (undated in that sentence); Gori's occupation 'lasted until 22 August'. The circles are the georgia dossier's (Gori 25 km, Zugdidi 30 km, Senaki 25 km) plus Poti (15 km), which the page names and the georgia circles miss; the page outlines no line, so the extent is the researcher's reading.

region.text: the same towns and buffer areas, evacuated on 8 October 2008

ledger.note: 8 October 2008: Russian forces leave the buffer areas. 'Russian forces pulled back from the buffer areas bordering Abkhazia and South Ossetia on 8 October 2008', 'to the line preceding the start of hostilities' under the agreement of 8 September, with the EU monitoring mission overseeing the areas. Georgia records the same end in October 2008 (georgia /ledger/18).

region.text: Crimea and the city of Sevastopol: 'the Republic of Crimea and federal city of Sevastopol'

ledger.note: 27 February 2014: Russian troops take Crimea. 'On 27 February, Russian special forces without insignia seized strategic sites across Crimea'; 'Russia formally incorporated Crimea on 18 March 2014 as the Republic of Crimea and federal city of Sevastopol'; UNGA 68/262 (27 March 2014, 100-11-58) affirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity. Annexed by Russia, drawn as occupied land.

region.text: 'almost all of Kherson Oblast, and about 70% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast' held when Russia annexed them

ledger.note: February 2022 onward: Russia occupies the south of Ukraine. The page gives the holdings at annexation ('about 60% of Donetsk Oblast, most of Luhansk Oblast, almost all of Kherson Oblast, and about 70% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast') and the full-scale invasion of 24 February 2022 (Russo-Ukrainian war page); the capture dates of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia are not given, and the whole-oblast region over-states the Zaporizhzhia share (a gap-filler should draw the 70%).

region.text: the places Russian forces captured north of Kyiv in February-March 2022: Chernobyl and Pripyat, Bucha, Hostomel, Vorzel, half of Irpin, and Trostianets in Sumy Oblast

ledger.note: 24 February 2022: Russian forces cross into Kyiv, Chernihiv, Sumy and Zhytomyr oblasts. 'On 24 February 2022 ... the Russian military crossed the' border 'entering the oblasts (regions) of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Sumy, and Zhytomyr'; they 'captured the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant and the ghost city of Pripyat', Trostianets 'was occupied by a garrison of Russian troops on 1 March', 'capturing Bucha, Hostomel, and Vorzel by 5 March' and 'half of Irpin by 14 March'. Kyiv, Chernihiv (encircled 10 March) and Sumy were never taken and the page outlines no front line, so the region is circles at the places it says were captured (the researcher's reading, not whole oblasts).

region.text: the east of Kharkiv Oblast held by Russia from late February 2022: Shevchenkove, Kupiansk, Balakliia, Izium and Vovchansk and their surroundings

ledger.note: 26 February 2022 onward: Russian forces occupy the east of Kharkiv Oblast. 'Shevchenkove came under Russian occupation on 26 February 2022', Kupiansk 'on 27 February', Balakliia 'on 2 March', and 'in early April, Russian forces captured Izium'; Russian forces also held Vovchansk. Kharkiv city was never taken. The region is circles at the named towns cut to the oblast (47 cells, about 11,900 km2, against the page's 'over 500 settlements and 12,000 square kilometers' retaken): the researcher's reading, since the page draws no line.

region.text: the same places, evacuated by Russian forces

ledger.note: Late March - early April 2022: Russia withdraws from north of Kyiv. 'Russia withdrew its forces from Kyiv, Zhytomyr, Chernihiv and Sumy oblasts in late March and early April 2022, and Ukrainian forces retook control'; 'Ukrainian forces entered' Bucha 'on 1 April'; the infobox dates the campaign '24 February - 8 April 2022'. The war page: Russia 'abandoned an attempt to seize Kyiv in early April'. The month is the page's 'early April'.

region.text: the east of Kharkiv Oblast retaken by Ukraine in September 2022, as occupied from February

ledger.note: September 2022: Ukraine's Kharkiv counteroffensive ends the occupation. 'On 6 September 2022, the Armed Forces of Ukraine launched a major counteroffensive'; Balakliia and Shevchenkove were retaken the next day, 'on 10 September, Ukrainian forces retook Kupiansk and Izium', and by 13 September Ukraine had retaken 'all of Kharkiv Oblast west of the Oskil River'. The Russo-Ukrainian war page: 'recaptured the majority of Kharkiv Oblast in September'. Typed occupation_end (it was typed loss before review) because the land was carried as occupation from February 2022; Russian forces kept the ground east of the Oskil.

region.text: Luhansk Oblast, held mostly by Russia and the LPR

ledger.note: 30 September 2022: Russia annexes the Luhansk People's Republic. 'On 30 September, Putin signed accession treaties with the four pro-Russian leaders of the regions' and 'unilaterally declared its annexation'; the State Duma ratified on 3 October; UNGA ES-11/4 (12 October 2022) voted 143-5-35 against. Russia recognised the LPR and DPR on 21 February 2022; Peskov said they would be annexed in 'their 2014 borders'. Revised after review: the 2024 keyframe now carries this land in the Russian solid, in agreement with this gain and the republic's dissolve event.

region.text: the Donetsk People's Republic, about 60% of Donetsk Oblast, as in the DPR dossier's 2022 extent

ledger.note: 30 September 2022: Russia annexes the Donetsk People's Republic with its 2022 gains ('about 60% of Donetsk Oblast' held). Not recognised internationally (UNGA ES-11/4, 143 in favour of condemning, 5 against, 35 abstaining). The region is the one the DPR dossier uses for its 2022 extent. Revised after review: the 2024 keyframe now carries this land in the Russian solid, in agreement with this gain and the republic's dissolve event.

region.text: the right bank of the Dnieper in Kherson Oblast, from which Russia withdrew: Kherson and its surroundings, Snihurivka, Beryslav, Davydiv Brid and Dudchany

ledger.note: 9-11 November 2022: Russia withdraws from Kherson and the right bank. 'On 9 November, Russian troops were ordered to withdraw from Kherson'; 'Russia announced the withdrawal of its troops from Kherson and the right bank of the Dnieper'; 'On 11 November, Ukrainian troops entered the city of Kherson'; the annexation page: 'including Kherson on 11 November 2022'. Typed occupation_end (it was typed loss before review) because the land is carried as occupation (the 2022-2 occupation of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia). The region is circles at the right-bank towns the page names, cut to the oblast (28 cells, about 7,100 km2); Davydiv Brid and Dudchany had been retaken on 4 October, earlier than the withdrawal, and the event is dated at the withdrawal. The page gives no line, so the extent is the researcher's reading; Nova Kakhovka and the left bank stay Russian.

region.text: the part of Kursk Oblast around Sudzha entered by Ukraine ('an area of up to 350 square kilometres'), a 15 km circle cut to the oblast

ledger.note: August 2024: Ukraine enters Kursk Oblast. 'In August 2024, the Ukrainian Armed Forces launched an incursion into Russia's Kursk Oblast', capturing 'an area of up to 350 square kilometres' (Ukrainian claim). The fighting is not ended on the page. Revised after review: the zone was the whole of Kursk Oblast (123 cells, about 31,100 km2) and is now a 15 km circle around Sudzha cut to the oblast (3 cells, about 760 km2). The Ukrainian incursion page (reopened) says the aim was 'Oleshnya in the direction of Sudzha', Syrskyi's claim of 'over 1,000 km2' and Zelenskyy's of 'Ukrainian forces ... 1,250 square kilometers' at the mid-August peak, the Russian recapture of Sudzha on 13 March 2025 and Ukraine's withdrawal from it on 16 March 2025; this dossier does not yet end the contest (outside the revision's scope).

wars.name: First Chechen War
wars.outcome: Russia took most of Chechnya by May 1995 but lost the initiative in August 1996; the Khasavyurt Accord of 31 August 1996 deferred Chechnya's status to 2001 and federal forces withdrew by the end of 1996.
wars.note: Infobox 11 December 1994 - 31 August 1996; peace treaty 'on peace and the principles of Russian-Chechen relations' signed 12 May 1997.

wars.name: Second Chechen War
wars.outcome: Russia reconquered Chechnya in the main phase (7 August 1999 - 30 April 2000), imposed direct rule in May 2000 and ended its counter-terrorism operation on 16 April 2009; the separatists were reduced to an insurgency.
wars.note: The territorial change is 1999-2000; the years to 2009 are the insurgency.

wars.name: Russo-Ukrainian war

zones.text: the places north of Kyiv held from 24 February to early April 2022
east Kharkiv Oblast, held from February to September 2022
the Ukrainian foothold around Sudzha in Kursk Oblast, from 6 August 2024

wars.outcome: Russia occupied Crimea in 2014 and, after the 24 February 2022 invasion, about 'roughly 20%' of Ukraine; it proclaimed the annexation of four oblasts on 30 September 2022; Ukraine retook Kharkiv Oblast (September 2022) and Kherson (11 November 2022). Ongoing.
wars.note: Front lines year by year after 2022 are not on the pages opened; see the notes. Revised after review: zones added for the north of Kyiv, east Kharkiv Oblast and the (narrowed) Kursk foothold; the Kursk zone had been the whole oblast in the ledger.

wars.name: Russo-Georgian War

zones.text: Abkhazia, recognised by Russia on 26 August 2008
South Ossetia (the part of it in Cliopatria's shape)
the Georgian towns Russia occupied outside the two regions: Zugdidi, Senaki, Poti and Gori (to 8 October 2008)
the Akhalgori district and the Georgian villages near Tskhinvali, lost to South Ossetian forces (Akhalgori 'occupied' by them after 17 August)
the Upper Kodori Valley, bombarded from 9 August and attacked by Abkhaz forces about 12 August

wars.outcome: Russia invaded Georgia's undisputed territory on 8 August 2008 ('1-16 August 2008' in the infobox; ceasefire negotiated by Sarkozy on 12 August); it occupied Zugdidi, Senaki, Poti and Gori and pulled back from the buffer areas on 8 October 2008; Georgia lost the Kodori Valley, Akhalgori Municipality and parts of the Tskhinvali District; Russia recognised Abkhazia and South Ossetia on 26 August 2008.
wars.note: Reopened for the revision (the first version had no zones because the war page was not opened). Akhalgori is dated only by the sequence 'New checkpoints were erected by the Russian forces on the Tbilisi-Gori road on 17 August ... South Ossetian forces occupied Akhalgori'. The occupation layer of Abkhazia and South Ossetia is the ledger's 2008-8 event; the buffer-zone events mirror georgia.

certainty.note: The post-Soviet frontiers follow the Soviet republic and oblast lines and later treaties. Exceptions: Chechnya in 1994-1996 and 1999-2000 (contested, soft), the Crimean and Donbas lines and the southern front since 2022 (occupation or annexation lines, soft), and the Kursk foothold in 2024.

notes:
Russian Federation, written by eu-22-g on 2026-11-01 from seven pages (five for this state, two shared with the ukraine and russian-occupied-territories dossiers).

Cliopatria rows reviewed (six shapes): the shapes are one outline that differs only by Chechnya (17,387 km2 in 1996-1999 and 2006-2013) and Crimea (21,857 km2 from 2014). The Chechnya years are wrong: Cliopatria leaves Chechnya out in 1992-1995 and 2000-2005 and puts it in during 1996-1999 and from 2006, the reverse of what the First and Second Chechen War pages say (independent 1996-autumn 1999, Russian from 2000). The verdicts correct that; the Chechen Republic row (eu-19) needs the matching review.

Crimea and the 2022 annexations: the project's scope draws Crimea and the Donbas after 2014 as occupied or contested land, so the 2014 shape is cut back to the 2006-2013 outline and Crimea (and, from 2022, almost all of Kherson Oblast and about 70% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast) are occupation_start events with Ukraine as owner. The annexation of the Donetsk and Luhansk republics on 30 September 2022 is recorded as a gain from their rebel dossiers, matching their dissolve events; that treats those two oblast parts as Russian solid while Crimea is hatched, an inconsistency settled in the revision below. The occupation_start and contest_start events for 2014 Crimea, 2022 and 2024 have no end because they are open at the end of the data; the validator warns about them.

What the pages did not give: the war fronts of 2022-2024 beyond the annexation holdings, the capture dates of Kherson city and Melitopol (early 2022), the 2014-2015 Donbas front (carried by the donetsk-people-s-republic and luhansk-people-s-republic dossiers), Russian garrisons in Transnistria (the page says 'since 1992', no month) and the August 2008 war (no page opened). The Russia page gives no dates of presidential terms, so no ruler strip is given. Border treaties (China 2004/2008, Norway 2010) are not on the Russia page and are not recorded.

Two guessed titles for the 2022 annexation page failed (url_not_found); the title 'Russian annexation of Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts' loaded.

Region names the gazetteer may lack: none beyond Natural Earth spellings (Crimea and Sevastopol are listed under Russia in Natural Earth 10m).

Revision of 2026-11-01 (after the adversarial review; fixes applied from reopened pages). (1) Donbas treatment settled: the annexed Luhansk and Donetsk People's Republic lands are Russian solid from 30 September 2022 (the two September 2022 gains, which match the two republics' dissolve events in their own dossiers), so the 2024 keyframe is now the 2013 outline plus those lands. Crimea and the occupied south stay hatched occupation of Ukraine. The reviewer's other choice (retype the two September 2022 gains as occupation_start with counterpart ukraine) would leave the two republics' dissolve events without a mirror and the ukraine dossier's losses to them unanswered, and the reviewer's rider 'draw Crimea the same way' contradicts the project scope that draws Crimea as occupied land; the author therefore keeps the gains and records the difference. (2) Added the occupation north of Kyiv (24 February - early April 2022, Northern Ukraine campaign page) and of east Kharkiv Oblast (26 February - September 2022, 2022 Kharkiv counteroffensive page); retyped the September Kharkiv and November Kherson reversals as occupation_end; widened the Kherson region to the right-bank towns named on the 2022 Kherson counteroffensive page. (3) Narrowed the Kursk zone to a 15 km circle at Sudzha (3 cells). (4) Added the 2008 buffer-zone occupation (8 August - 8 October 2008) with the same circles as georgia plus Poti, and gave the Russo-Georgian War zones; whether Abkhazia and South Ossetia are Russian-occupied (this ledger, from the Russian-occupied territories page) or republic land (georgia's ledger) is for the georgia owner and the orchestrator. (5) The Russia infobox figure 17,098,246 km2 is qualified '(within internationally recognised borders)'; the keyframe note no longer says it includes Crimea. (6) Still open: the Chechnya 1995 loss (chechen-republic has none), the March 2025 end of the Kursk contest (the Ukrainian incursion page gives 13-16 March 2025), and the 2023-2024 front lines.
